title: Leon Max, Inc. v. Commissioner
articleTitle: The Judicial Narrowing of Innovation: Analyzing Leon Max, Inc. v. Commissioner and the Reshaping of the R&D Tax Credit Landscape
subject: Process of Experimentation
summary: Ruled that a fashion brand's fit-testing activities were aesthetic rather than technological, failing the fundamental R&D credit requirements.

body.text: The federal tax credit for increasing research activities, commonly referred to as the Research and Development (R&D) tax credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41, has historically served as a cornerstone of American industrial policy. Designed to incentivize domestic technological advancement, the credit has evolved from a relatively straightforward benefit for laboratory-based sciences into a complex, highly litigated area of tax law that permeates diverse sectors of the economy. However, recent judicial interpretations have signaled a significant tightening of the criteria necessary to qualify for these incentives, moving toward a more restrictive "hard science" and "scientific method" standard. The landmark case of Leon Max, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-37, stands as a critical inflection point in this evolution, particularly for creative and design-intensive industries. This case, decided by the United States Tax Court, provides an exhaustive examination of the boundaries between routine industrial design and qualified research, ultimately delivering a "scorched-earth" opinion that has far-reaching implications for taxpayers across the United States.
Historical and Statutory Context of the Section 41 Credit

To appreciate the gravity of the Leon Max decision, one must first locate it within the broader framework of the Internal Revenue Code. The R&D tax credit is an incremental credit, generally equal to 20% of the excess of a taxpayer’s "qualified research expenses" (QREs) for a taxable year over a base amount. Since its inception, the credit has been intended to reward activities that involve a high degree of technical risk and innovation. The definition of "qualified research" is governed by a rigorous four-part test under Section 41(d)(1), which must be applied at the level of each discrete "business component"—a term encompassing products, processes, computer software, techniques, formulas, or inventions.

The statutory history of Section 41 reveals a persistent tension between the legislative intent to foster broad innovation and the administrative desire to prevent the credit from becoming a subsidy for routine business operations. This tension is most evident in the interplay between Section 41 and Section 174. While Section 174 allows for the deduction (or, post-2022, the amortization) of research and experimental expenditures, Section 41 provides a dollar-for-dollar credit, but only for a subset of those expenditures that meet additional, more stringent technical criteria.

cells: Expenditures must be deductible as R&E expenses, focusing on the elimination of uncertainty.
Research must be undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature.
Substantially all activities must involve a systematic process to evaluate alternatives.
The research must relate to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality.

body.text: The application of this four-part test has been the primary battleground for recent litigation, with the IRS strategically selecting cases to fight through trial, particularly those involving smaller businesses and credits under $1 million. Leon Max, Inc. v. Commissioner represents a successful effort by the Commissioner to establish a high bar for "technological" discovery and "experimentation" in the creative design space.
Factual Underpinnings of Leon Max, Inc. v. Commissioner

Leon Max, an immigrant who established a successful fashion empire in Los Angeles, operated Leon Max, Inc. (LMI) as an S-corporation. The firm designed and produced high-end women's clothing under brands like Max Studio and Leon Max, sold through major retail channels and boutique stores. For the 2011 and 2012 tax years, LMI claimed R&D credits of $426,255 and $496,462, respectively, which were passed through to Leon Max’s individual returns. The IRS challenged these credits, leading to a trial that delved deeply into the minutiae of the fashion design process.

The taxpayer's argument centered on the idea that the creation of high-end apparel is not merely an artistic endeavor but a technical one involving material science, textile engineering, and complex problem-solving. LMI's development process was categorized into several distinct stages, which the company claimed involved technical uncertainty and experimentation:

items: Concept and Design: The process began with "mood boards" and conceptual sketches aimed at capturing a seasonal aesthetic.

Technical Sketching and Patternmaking: Designers created "blueprints" of garment components. Patternmakers then translated these sketches into physical components, selecting trims, linings, and thread.

Sample Creation and Fit Testing: This stage involved creating a prototype garment and testing it on a "fit model." Judge Buch's opinion noted the precision of this stage, where models were asked to mimic activities like "driving a car, holding a baby, or reaching for an item on a high shelf" to evaluate movement and comfort.
Material Testing: LMI performed various tests on fabrics, including washing for shrinkage, steaming for texture, and "tugging" for durability.
Scaling and Production: Adjusting patterns for "plus-size" garments and ensuring print alignment across different sizes was presented as an engineering challenge.

body.text: The Tax Court was unpersuaded by the technical framing of these activities. The opinion, which spans 21 pages of detailed analysis of garmentry, famously suggests that while the petitioner's clothing was worthy of praise, his tax strategies were not.
The Judicial Deconstruction of the Four-Part Test in Leon Max
The court's decision hinged on a rigorous, and some argue "scorched-earth," application of the four-part test, systematically dismantling the taxpayer’s assertions for each requirement.
The Failure of the Section 174 Uncertainty Test

The first hurdle, the Section 174 test, requires that expenditures be incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development costs in the "experimental or laboratory sense". Uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product or the "appropriate design" of the product.

LMI argued that it faced significant uncertainties regarding how to cut and drape printed fabrics, the choice of thread sizes, fabric shrinkage, and the final fit of the garment. The court, however, ruled that these did not constitute "uncertainties" under the law. The reasoning was twofold: first, the court found that LMI's employees—patternmakers and designers—already possessed the necessary information and skill to address these issues as they arose. For instance, LMI required new hires to prove they could handle tasks like print alignment and fabric cutting before they were permanently employed, which the court viewed as evidence that these were standard industry problems with known solutions.

Second, the court categorized LMI's testing—such as washing fabric to check for shrinkage—as "quality control" rather than "investigative" research. Under Section 174 and its regulations, quality control testing, which is performed to ensure a product meets its intended specifications after design uncertainty is resolved, is specifically excluded from the definition of research expenditures. The court found that LMI's "prescribed standards from recognized industry organizations" meant that the testing was a routine part of ensuring a high-quality product, not an exploration of unknown technical frontiers.
The "Hard Science" Barrier: The Technological Information Test

The second part of the test requires that the research be undertaken to discover information that is "technological in nature". This means the research must fundamentally rely on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

LMI made an aggressive attempt to frame fashion design as a scientific discipline, arguing that fit testing was essentially "engineering," draping fabric was "material science," and shrinkage testing was "chemistry". The court's rejection of this argument was blunt, stating that such assertions "defy a common understanding of words and terms".

cells: Engineering involves the application of science to manufacture "complex products" like bridges or satellites.
While "draping coefficients" exist in material science, LMI did not use them; they just draped fabric to see how it looked.
Chemistry implies "fundamentally changing the structure" of materials; washing a fabric is a routine household activity.

body.text: The court’s analogy regarding the physics of baseball—that a centerfielder is not a mathematician just because a formula exists for the flight of a ball—underscored its view that using a product (fabric) does not equate to scientific research into that product's fundamental properties. This sets a daunting precedent for any industry where technical knowledge is applied through intuition or "craft" rather than through formal scientific equations and laboratory protocols.
The Systematic Process of Experimentation and the "Scientific Method"

The third requirement—the process of experimentation—proved to be the most contentious. This test requires that substantially all of the activities constitute a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. The Tax Court in Leon Max asserted that a "true" process of experimentation must use the "scientific method". This involves a methodical plan including:

items: Conducting a series of trials to test that hypothesis.

body.text: The court found that LMI’s process was a "thorough integration of a creative development process" rather than a systematic scientific inquiry. While LMI engaged in trial and error—adjusting a pattern or changing a thread size—the court distinguished "simple trial and error" from the "systematic trial and error" required by the regulations. Critics of the opinion point out that Treasury Regulation §1.41-4(a)(5)(i) specifically allows for systematic trial and error and does not explicitly mandate the formal "scientific method" as traditionally defined in laboratory settings. However, the Leon Max decision, following the lead of cases like Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, effectively narrows the definition of experimentation to a level that may be unreachable for many commercial R&D projects.
The Exclusion of Style, Taste, and Seasonality

Finally, the court addressed the statutory exclusion under IRC Section 41(d)(3)(B), which states that a "qualified purpose" does not include style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. This is perhaps the most significant hurdle for the apparel industry. LMI argued that its activities were focused on the "function" of the garments, such as their fit and durability. The court disagreed, reasoning that because the primary purpose of designing a seasonal clothing line is aesthetic and style-driven, the activities cannot satisfy the "qualified purpose" element. The court noted that "the function of all pants is essentially the same: to stay up and cover the wearer... Every other consideration... is one of cosmetics".

Because the taxpayer could not prove that at least 80% of its activities were for a qualified purpose (the "substantially all" requirement), the entire claim failed. The court's focus on the "all-or-nothing" nature of the 80% rule emphasizes the risk of claiming credits for a business component that has significant non-qualifying elements.
Comparative Analysis: Leon Max vs. Siemer Milling and Little Sandy Coal

The Leon Max decision is part of a trilogy of recent cases—including Siemer Milling Company v. Commissioner and Little Sandy Coal Company, Inc. v. Commissioner—that collectively signal a heightened documentation and technical burden for taxpayers.
Documentation and the Retrospective Study Problem

In all three cases, the taxpayers faced significant challenges regarding substantiation. Siemer Milling (2019) involved a wheat miller whose credits were denied because it failed to provide documentation showing a "methodical plan" for its production improvements. The court in Siemer Milling emphasized that simply reciting steps or making conclusory statements about being "technical" is insufficient; contemporaneous evidence, such as emails, test logs, and data analysis, is required.

Little Sandy Coal (2021) involved a shipbuilder whose claim was denied due to a lack of documentation linking employee time to specific technical uncertainties. The Seventh Circuit, in its 2023 appeal of Little Sandy Coal, affirmed that "shortcut estimates" and retrospective "trust me" studies will not suffice. This aligns with the Leon Max ruling, where the court rejected the taxpayer's reliance on a study conducted by an outside consultant years after the fact.

cells: Technical activities must follow the "scientific sense."
Failure to track time to subcomponents.
"All or nothing" strategies are high risk; use the shrink-back rule.
Generic time estimates and non-technical narratives.
Common knowledge and aesthetic goals disqualify research.

body.text: The 80% Rule and the Seventh Circuit's Intervention

A critical distinction arose in the appeal of Little Sandy Coal regarding the calculation of the "substantially all" (80%) threshold. The Tax Court in both Leon Max and the original Little Sandy Coal decision had suggested that direct supervision and support activities (such as a manager overseeing a researcher or a technician preparing a sample) did not count toward the "experimentation" numerator in the 80% fraction.

The Seventh Circuit reversed this in the Little Sandy Coal appeal, ruling that if the support and supervision are themselves part of the research process, they should be included in both the numerator and the denominator. This is a rare "taxpayer-friendly" development in an otherwise restrictive landscape, as it makes it mathematically easier to reach the 80% threshold for a business component. However, this victory is hollow without the contemporaneous documentation to prove that those support activities were indeed part of a process of experimentation.
Implications for Future R&D Tax Credit Applications in the USA

The Leon Max decision, when viewed alongside recent IRS enforcement trends, provides a roadmap for the future of R&D tax credit compliance. The "hard science" requirement and the "scientific method" standard are now the baseline expectations for any credit claim.
The Death of the "Retrospective Narrative"

The era of the high-level, retrospective R&D study is effectively over. Taxpayers can no longer rely on narratives created by consultants that "re-frame" routine business activities as scientific research after the fact. The IRS and the courts now demand a "nexus" between the qualified research expenses (QREs) and the specific business components. This requires:

items: Contemporaneous Documentation: Maintaining records at the time the research is performed, including project logs, design iterations, and testing protocols.
Activity-Based Time Tracking: Moving away from "generic estimates" of employee time toward specific systems that link hours spent to the resolution of technical uncertainty.
Technical Evidence: Preserving the "failed" prototypes and the "data" that led to refinements, proving that the process was truly experimental and not just a linear path to a known result.

body.text: Strategic Use of the "Shrink-Back Rule"

The Leon Max case highlights the danger of claiming a credit for a large business component (like an entire garment or an entire software platform) that contains significant non-qualifying elements like aesthetic design or routine maintenance. The "shrink-back rule" under Treasury Regulation §1.41-4(b)(2) allows taxpayers to apply the four-part test to increasingly smaller subcomponents.

If a fashion company cannot meet the 80% test for a new dress because much of the work was style-related, it might still qualify for the credit if it can isolate the development of a specific new technical fabric or a specific new manufacturing technique and prove that those sub-projects independently satisfy the four-part test. Future success in the apparel, software, and creative industries will depend on the ability to "shrink back" to the truly technological cores of their projects.
The Role and Risk of Outside Consultants

The Leon Max opinion noted the involvement of the advisory firm alliantgroup, which conducted the R&D study for LMI. The court's rejection of this study highlights the risk of relying on "study-based" documentation that may not align with the strict legal definitions of engineering and science. Taxpayers are advised to engage with advisors who understand the specific technical nuances of their industry and who can help implement the necessary contemporaneous documentation systems, rather than just delivering a retrospective report.
Impact on Non-Traditional R&D Industries

The "hard science" requirement in Leon Max creates a significant hurdle for industries like software development, food and beverage, and architecture, where much of the "innovation" is iterative and functional but may not involve "fundamental changes to the structure of materials" or "complex engineering" as defined by the court. Taxpayers in these sectors must be prepared to demonstrate how their work relies on the "principles of hard sciences" rather than just "existing knowledge and standard industry techniques".

The court's definition of engineering as relating only to "complex products" like bridges and satellites is particularly concerning for software developers, as it may be used by the IRS to argue that routine software iteration is not "engineering". Taxpayers should be prepared to fight this "complexity" requirement, as it does not appear in the statutory or regulatory language.
Technical Nuances: Amortization and Computational Mechanics
The strategic importance of the Leon Max decision is compounded by recent legislative changes regarding the treatment of research and experimental (R&E) expenditures.
Section 174 Amortization and the TCJA

Under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) of 2017, for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, taxpayers are no longer permitted to immediately deduct R&E expenditures. Instead, they must amortize these costs over five years for domestic research and fifteen years for foreign research.

This change increases the "cost" of a failed R&D credit claim. If an activity is classified as R&D but fails the Section 41 credit test (as in Leon Max), the taxpayer may still be forced to amortize the expenses under Section 174 if they meet the "uncertainty" test, leading to a significant deferral of tax benefits. Conversely, if the court rules (as it did in Leon Max) that the activities are not research at all but rather routine production or quality control, the taxpayer may be able to deduct them as ordinary business expenses under Section 162, avoiding the five-year amortization requirement of Section 174.
The 80% Rule Numerator and Denominator
Following the Seventh Circuit’s ruling in Little Sandy Coal, the calculation for the "substantially all" test is as follows:
$$\text{Experimentation Percentage} = \frac{\text{Directly Engaged Activities} + \text{Direct Support} + \text{Direct Supervision}}{\text{Total Research Activities}}$$

Previously, the IRS and the Tax Court (in Leon Max) had effectively removed the "Direct Support" and "Direct Supervision" from the numerator, making the 80% threshold much harder to hit. While the numerator is now more inclusive, the taxpayer must still document that every person included in that numerator was indeed supporting a process of experimentation (hypothesis testing) and not just routine production.
Professional Ethics and Practitioner Standards

The Leon Max decision also serves as a warning to tax practitioners. The "scorched-earth" nature of the opinion, with its "subtle burns" and detailed critiques of the taxpayer's logic, suggests that the Tax Court is losing patience with aggressive R&D claims that lack technical substance.
Practitioners must ensure that their R&D analyses align with the prescribed IRS framework, especially considering the upcoming changes to Form 6765. This includes:

items: Defining Technical Uncertainty Precisely: Avoiding generic statements and focusing on specific technical challenges that were not resolvable with existing knowledge.
Disqualifying Routine Work Upfront: Proactively excluding aesthetic design, code compliance, and quality control from the credit claim to preserve the credibility of the overall application.
Establishing the Nexus: Ensuring that every dollar claimed can be traced through business records to a specific research activity and a specific business component.

body.text: Future Outlook: A New Baseline for Innovation

The case of Leon Max, Inc. v. Commissioner is more than just a defeat for a single fashion company; it is a fundamental redefinition of what the U.S. government is willing to subsidize through the research tax credit. By demanding a "formalized scientific method" and a "hard science" foundation, the court has narrowed the gateway to these incentives.

For the apparel industry and other "creative" sectors, the path forward requires a shift from artistic intuition to technical documentation. For the broader taxpayer base, the case reinforces the necessity of contemporaneous records and project-based accounting. As the IRS continues to overhaul its reporting forms and strategically litigate cases involving estimated studies, the "common solutions to common problems" that undid Leon Max's claim will likely remain the primary target for future disallowances. Innovation, in the eyes of the Tax Court, is no longer just about the creation of something "new"; it is about the scientific rigor of the process used to create it.
